editorial_note: Ten original authored questions; source, key and distractor semantics checked against final Chapter 6 after the Day 30 navigation update. This technical check is not independent human approval or translation release. The site adds the fifth uncertainty choice and ten-second timing.

questions.prompt: C13 finds S42 version 19 unavailable and last request q-144. Which conclusion does that read support?

options.text: The shared account user was malicious.
The screenshot clock was independently verified.
The supplied authoritative read supports the stored state and request reference.
Every affected learner has been counted.

questions.explanation: C confines the result to the custodian's owner-approved state read and its supplied request reference; the separate 08:30 snapshot supports a state difference. A invents human intent. B confuses backend evidence with C10 capture context. D invents an impact denominator. The read does not itself authorize a hold or restore.
questions.source: Chapter 6, Week 6 / course Day 26, #week-06-day-01, impact/state paragraphs and four-row practice; §6.2 C13; EX026.

questions.prompt: C14 excludes q-144 from a complete manifest for one approved batch-17 run. What is the bounded inference?

options.text: That specified run manifest does not contain q-144.
No automated task could have issued q-144.
A human attacker must have issued q-144.
Every scheduler inventory is now complete.

questions.explanation: A uses the supplied completeness and API-namespace premise for this one run. B generalizes beyond that source to all automation. C converts a bounded exclusion into human attribution and intent. D enlarges one-run completeness to a system-wide inventory. C12's self-reported tag is weakened as origin evidence without identifying another producer.
questions.source: Chapter 6, Week 6 / course Day 26, #week-06-day-01, C14 bounded-manifest paragraph; §6.2 C14; EX026.

questions.prompt: At 09:35, C16 says an initial ten-minute S42 hold would be tolerable. What has it supplied?

options.text: An execution receipt for g-22.
Approval to disable svc-enroll.
A verified all-route containment result.
Initial impact tolerance for a conditional proposal.

questions.explanation: D preserves the role of C16 as planning input about legitimate interruption. A requires an operator operation record, supplied later as C18. B broadens the target and invents authority. C requires route-specific observations that tolerance cannot provide. C17 is a distinct later S42-only approval, not implied by C16.
questions.source: Chapter 6, Week 6 / course Day 27, #week-06-day-02, worked recommendation and limits; §6.2 C16; EX027.

questions.prompt: Why might restricting only s-77 fail to prevent another q-144-like S42 write at the 09:35 checkpoint?

options.text: Session restrictions can never reduce harm.
The supplied records lack a direct session-to-request join.
C16 proves the entire account must be disabled.
A revoked session automatically repairs S42 state.

questions.explanation: B identifies the unsupported benefit premise: even a verified session revocation might not affect the harmful write path. A turns a local uncertainty into a universal rule. C mistakes tolerance for broad authority and ignores shared-account service cost. D confuses credential/session restriction with business-state repair. Compare all three controls against the same harm and independent service gates.
questions.source: Chapter 6, Week 6 / course Day 27, #week-06-day-02, causal-path explanation and three-control table; EX027.

questions.prompt: Which action scope is actually approved by C17 at 09:37?

options.text: S42-only write hold expiring at 09:47.
Account-wide disablement until attribution is complete.
Restoration of the 08:30 slot snapshot.
A fresh ten minutes from any eventual deployment time.

questions.explanation: A names the target and fixed expiry of the fictional approval, with its operator, monitoring and rollback obligations. B invents a broader target and indefinite duration. C substitutes a data restore for the approved guard. D silently resets expiry rather than obtaining new authority. The approval does not itself prove deployment or effect.
questions.source: Chapter 6, Week 6 / course Day 28, #week-06-day-03, four-checkpoint narrative and clock contrast; §6.4 C17; EX028.

questions.prompt: C18 reports g-22 enabled at 09:39. Which status should the responder record from that receipt alone?

options.text: Every mutation route independently tested.
All harmful access permanently removed.
Operator-reported enablement; protective effect still needs observation.
Actual rollback and service restoration completed.

questions.explanation: C identifies an execution report and leaves verification distinct. A requires coverage observations beyond the receipt. B adds durable all-access eradication unsupported by a guard change. D invents reversal and recovery. Even C19's later selective observations establish a narrower result than all-route effectiveness.
questions.source: Chapter 6, Week 6 / course Day 28, #week-06-day-03, learning task and worked record; §6.4 C18; EX028.

questions.prompt: C19 records q-147/S42 denied on one application route and q-148/S40 accepted. What is still unverified?

options.text: Whether the supplied S40 request was accepted.
Whether the supplied S42 request was denied.
Whether C19 contains the two stated observations.
Alternate-route coverage and S41 behavior.

questions.explanation: D names missing coverage rather than erasing supplied observations. A and B contradict the stated results; C denies the supplied record itself. One S40 success does not establish S41, and one S42 denial does not establish every API/database/job path. Unknown routes are neither proven bypasses nor proven denials.
questions.source: Chapter 6, Week 6 / course Day 28, #week-06-day-03, C19 paragraph and worked record; Day 29, #week-06-day-04, denominator contrast; EX028.

questions.prompt: Using 09:39 reported enablement and the fixed 09:47 expiry, what does W6-TIME calculate?

options.text: Ten minutes of independently proven protection.
Eight minutes in the reported window, without proof of continuous enforcement.
A new expiry at 09:49 under the original approval.
Coverage that includes an observation exactly at 09:47.

questions.explanation: B is the eight-minute arithmetic bound under same-day UTC inputs, not effect evidence. A confuses the approval-to-expiry interval with protection. C resets the fixed expiry. D violates the laboratory's half-open interval: exact expiry is OUTSIDE_REPORTED_WINDOW. Interval membership cannot authenticate authority, activation or route coverage.
questions.source: Chapter 6, Week 6 / course Day 28, #week-06-day-03, Offline W6-TIME program, exact transcript and limitation paragraph; EX028.

questions.prompt: V6 denies a browser S42 write, accepts a direct API S42 write and passes S40. What is its verdict?

options.text: All-route containment passes because S40 works.
CTN has a proven API bypass and must disable its account.
The isolated all-route S42 property fails despite the service control passing.
The untested CTN routes are all proven denied.

questions.explanation: C evaluates V6's declared protected-operation criterion: one accepted prohibited route defeats it, independently of the S40 control. A lets business success cancel protection failure. B imports a separate fixture result into CTN and invents authority. D turns unknown coverage into a pass. C6X similarly separates PROTECTION_FAIL from BUSINESS_FAIL; its toy BASE/pass inputs are not production assurance.
questions.source: Chapter 6, Week 6 / course Day 29, #week-06-day-04, worked V6 verdict and C6X laboratory review; §§6.5/6.15; EX030.

questions.prompt: At 09:42, which rollback-card entry is supported without inventing a later operation or renewal?

options.text: Record 09:47 expiry and owner-governed triggers; leave actual reversal/results pending.
Record rollback completed because a timer is scheduled.
Extend the hold automatically until the incident closes.
Restore the 08:30 database snapshot to undo g-22.

questions.explanation: A distinguishes conditional planning from executed reversal and retains scope, preserved evidence, owner/operator roles and post-action checks. B invents a receipt and service result. C invents renewal beyond the fixed authority. D confuses a guard reversal with overwriting business data. A bypass can require urgent re-planning rather than automatic removal of a partly protective control; any expansion needs actual authority.
questions.source: Chapter 6, Week 6 / course Day 30, #week-06-day-05, trigger comparison, contrast and 09:42 handoff; EX029.
